samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Walter Stevens was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: Well, I see here you were a Chief Machinist's Mate?

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: And I'm glad that you're Navy, cause I'm Navy, and these two Air Force people here have been beating up on me, Walt.

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: That's okay. They're Service, too.

sp.speaker: Videographer
sp.p: Okay, you are set to go.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: Okay, wait a minute. Ready to go? Okay.

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: I'm Walter L. Stevens. I was born in Catlin, New York. It's a township -- small village. When I was two years old, my family moved to -- to Pennsylvania, and that's where I grew up, on a farm, until I joined the Navy in 1935. I enlisted in Elmira, New York, substation, but I swore in in Buffalo, New York, the main recruiting station. They sent me on a train to Norfolk, Virginia for training.

I went through the Norfolk, Virginia Naval Training Station. From there, after two or three weeks after graduation, I was sent to the USS Semmes. That was four-stack destroyer, World War One. Formerly, it was DD 189, but it had been made into a experimental ship for sonar. We had sonar gear on board and we experimented with submarine on the sonar situation, the development of it.

In October 1936, I was transferred to a new destroyer, the USS Lamson, DD367 in Boston, Massachusetts at the time. The ship was built in Bath, Maine. We were in Boston a couple of months -- went on shakedown cruise to Brazil -- can't think of the name of the town, it wasn't Rio -- and then on to Buenos Aires, Argentina. We got to Buenos Aires in January 1937.

We had a nice time there and everything. Of course I was young in the Navy then, and those days we wore dress white jumpers, the ones with the stripes and stars on them in foreign ports. We came back from shakedown cruise, stopped at Barbados -- Bridgetown, Barbados -- for a few days, and then to Norfolk, Virginia. We were around the navy yard there in Norfolk for two or three months before they sent us to Panama, through the Panama Canal, up the west coast of Central America, Mexico, to San Diego, California.

We operated out of San Diego for two or three days when they sent us out in the Pacific looking for a ___, Holland Island. They sent us on the Lexington, the old Lexington aircraft carrier and several other destroyers. We was out there the biggest part of a month of July, and then back to Honolulu for a few days, and then back to San Diego. We operated with a fleet out of San Diego. In 1939, they sent us to the Atlantic for maneuvers. We were supposed to go to the World Fair in New York, but something happened in Europe, with the war in Europe, and they canceled that.

We went back to Panama and back to San Diego on the West Coast. We operated out of San Diego until September -- late September 1939. They sent us to Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. The whole fleet eventually come out there, most of all our ships. And we operated. In 1940, I was transferred to the USS Dobbin, a destroyer repair ship. I served on that until well after the war started. We worked on destroyers and did general repair work of all kinds until suddenly, on September 7, 1941, the Japs sneaked in on us and started bombing airplanes and torpedoing ships. It was a surprise to all of us. I was ashore at the time because that happened on a Sunday morning. I was First Class Machinist's Mate then and I ___ a weekend delivery, went ashore on Saturday.

I usually stayed until Sunday afternoon, but for some odd reason I've never been able to figure out, I decided to come back to the ship early in the morning. I had an old car. And let me see, I had over six years in the Navy at that time. I came up Camile (ph) Highway and I saw all the taxis and cars with sailors in them and everything. We got up to where the highway crosses the O'ahu Railroad. O'ahu Railroad was a narrow-gauge railroad used mostly for taking pineapples and sugar cane and that sort of thing to the factory in Honolulu. The road crosses right there, and traffic was stalled clear into Pearl Harbor Gate, over a mile, Hickam Field, the army air station and Pearl Harbor.

While I was standing in that line, I saw an airplane way off to my forward and to my left over Hickam Field, the army air field. When it turned up I saw those red balls on the wings and it just suddenly hit me: Those are Japanese planes. But I still didn't hardly realize they'd started a war. But I saw it drop a bomb in Hickam Field, and I knew right then that we must be under attack. The plane went off to my left and way down behind me. All the sudden it came right up that line of traffic with a machine gun. Went right past us.

A bullet went right through the front fender of my car on the driver's side, and blew a tire. I wasn't about to stand in that traffic line. And I hooked it into low gear, popped the clutch, went down through a ditch and right up I went up on O'ahu Railroad, a narrow-gate railroad.

I went up the railroad about, oh, a mile to a mile and a half over in the navy housing area just at the entrance to Pearl Harbor Gate, main gate. I abandoned the car there and ran into the -- through the gate. I was accepted through the gate all right -- my ID card. But just 40, 50, 100 feet beyond, all a sudden another plane come (strapping). Machine gun. There was a lieutenant with boatswain whites. We both hit the dirt right there on our bellies.

I remember a little town ___. He said: "I knew dang well that scrap iron we sold Japan was coming flying back at us one of these days." The plane bullets hit not far from us and went past. We both jumped up and ran our own ways. I took off for the fleet landing. I wanted to get a boat back to my ship. I got to the fleet landing.

There was a loud speaker calling for men to go down to the navy yard to the big dry dock where the Pennsylvania was on fire, and the destroyer Cassin and Downes had been bombed, to fight fire and pick up casualties. There wasn't any boats there, so I just took it on the run for that big dry dock in the navy yard. I ran all the way down there.

I helped pick up several casualties. One man come off one of those destroyers across the gang way, and the gang way was on fire. He just got across the gang way, and the gang way fell down in the dry dock. There was a Chief Petty Officer there helping pick up casualties. The ambulances had all been used and gone to the hospital. They had a flat-bed truck, a big truck there putting casualties on.

I helped put casualties on the truck. The Chief Petty Officer I noticed, when his back was toward me, he had a piece of shrapnel a foot long sticking right out of his back. But he was working. He was helping. When we got everybody loaded, I told him, "Boy, you lay down on your belly on that truck and don't you let anybody touch you till you get to the hospital and let the doctor take that out." Cause I said, "That's bad."

Then I took off running and went all the way back to the fleet landing. When I got back there, there was a 50-foot Maryland motor launch from the battleship Maryland there. And they was calling for help to fight fire around the West Virginia, or on it. The motor launch -- I got in the Maryland motor launch -- we went to the West Virginia, but we couldn't get near it. Everything was on fire. The oil on the surface of the water was on fire.

We finally picked up two guys that come swimming out from under, and then another plane smashed us -- punched two holes in the boat. I took it on myself to pull up a torch on the boat until I found an old screwdriver and a rag, and I started punching the rag into those holes. It was spouting water where the bullets went through. I looked up and I spotted a motor launch from my own ship, the USS Dobbin, 83. I hailed him. He come alongside and I finally got into the boat from my own ship.

We looked around to pick up casualties but didn't find any, so went back to the ship. I got back to my ship. Shortly before the attack was over -- boy I'll tell you, we was all hands carrying ammunition and working on machinery to get those destroyers alongside back in commission so they could go to sea. So we worked around the clock. I didn't even change out of uniform. That was the Pearl Harbor deal. And that was it. We worked for weeks with very little sleep -- all-hand. It was all-hands job. Everybody performed very nicely and did their job, and I heard no big complaints. That's my story of Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: Do you go on the rest of the war?

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: So what happened to you after Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: All right. I was aboard at the island on the 22nd of February. We still did a lot of repair work around Pearl Harbor, but on the 22nd of February -- Washington's birthday, and that's the reason I remember it -- we got on our way for the South Pacific headed for Samoa, (Atua), Samoa.

We had a submarine attack right around just after we crossed the equator. Two old World War One four-stack destroyers was escorting us, and they dropped dep charges and everything. A torpedo was shot at us. The captain turned the ship and the torpedo went right down our side, close aboard, but it never touched us. We was loaded with bombs and everything.

Torpedos, depth charges, you name it. Boy, we'd have still been flying if that thing ever went off. We went to Samoa. We operated there for, oh, a month or six weeks. There was a submarine, Japanese submarine attack on Samoa one night, but outside the harbor.

They shot shells in the harbor. Did very little damage. It hit one building, I think. Everything, but -- They rounded up -- evidently, there was a couple of two-man submarines. One of them did get through the nap and was dep-charged and sunk just inside that mouth of the harbor. The other submarine was caught in the nap. And they surfaced them the next day.

From Pearl Harbor, or, from Samoa, we headed for New Caledonia, I think. We was in the Coral Sea, when the Coral Sea battle took place. Now, the old repair ships were a good-size ship, but they had small engines. They wasn't a fast ship. We got the word to get out of there and go anyplace.

We ended up going to -- I can't think of the name of the island. I should be able to think of it. It was where the Yorktown came in after she had been bombed in the Coral Sea battle. Can't think of the name of that darned island right now. It's a small island that's sanctioned by New Zealand.

We was there for probably a month, and then we got on our way and went to Suva, Fiji Islands. We was only there a few hours, in Suva, and they sent us to Sydney, Australia. We went into Sydney, and of course the crew was anxious to go ashore, but there was a Japanese submarine attack that night in Sydney Harbor. I had the duty. The USS Chicago, heavy cruiser, was moored a way off to our right in the harbor.

A torpedo went right through between the Chicago and my ship. It went clear to the head of Circular Key, the harbor, and there it hit a ferry boat, an old, obsolete ferry boat that the Australians had used for common ___. The men that was wounded in the war in the Navy or in the Middle East, and they'd sent them home, they was well enough so they was out of the hospital, but they just put them on that ferry boat and let them take care of themselves until they got well enough for reassignment.

I spent a year there in Sydney. Made Chief Petty Officer, Chief Machinist's Mate, and was transferred back to the States where I took a new destroyer in commission up in Seattle, Washington. I went to Norfolk, Virginia first, for school -- pre-commissioning school, with a draft of men, then to Seattle, Washington where I went aboard the USS Critchen, DD 561. I served about four months on that, but down in the -- we went to the South Pacific and came back to Pearl.

A lot of time went past here and I sort of forget a little bit. They called for some chief to be transferred, and I volunteered, and they sent me to the Sterett, DD 407. I missed the Sterett -- went out of harbor, but I caught another ship, the Helm, heading the same direction, and they took me aboard. Went to Anawetok in the Martial Islands, I believe. And there they transferred me to the ship I was assigned to, the Sterett, DD407.

I served the rest of the war on the Sterett. They was getting ready for the invasion of Saipan, Rota, Tinian, Guam, the Marianas Islands campaign, and the Philippine Sea campaign. We was in all of that. We had a lot of shooting at Japanese airplanes. The fighting for the Marines on Saipan and those islands was bad. Us Navy wasn't too bad, except the Japanese airplanes.

They attacked the fleet. They come out of the Philippines and attacked the fleet. That was the period of time I think the whole fleet was credited with shooting down over four hundred Japanese planes in one day. And we got in some shooting. I can't say we shot down a plane, but we helped.

There were several ships shooting at planes, and they came out from the islands of Saipan and Guam, and also from the carriers in the Philippine Sea. So we had quite bit of action there. After that we -- my ship was sent back to Seattle, Washington for an overhaul period, for a couple of months, and after we left Seattle, went to San Diego for de-gauzing and a few things like pre-commission -- what do you call it -- getting the ship ready for combat again. And they sent us back to Hawaii.

We ended up missing Hawaii. We went right straight to the Philippines. We got in the Philippines during the Lete Gulf action. There is our first contact with suicide planes. They give us a bad time in the Philippines. The channels between the islands was fairly narrow. Those suicide planes, they stayed behind the mountains where our radar couldn't pick them up. When they come out of the mountains, they was coming pretty close to us, fast.

One night they hit an aircraft carrier -- what we called a baby, a Keiser ship, escort carrier. They hit one, knocked it out. They hit an ammunition ship and blew it up, everything. Tokyo Rose got on the air and she said " you guys might as well turn back. We sunk two thirds of your convoy and we'll get the rest of you." We got to figuring up just what we'd seen, and they had knocked out pretty close to one third. She just doubled it and everything, but we kept right on going to the island of -- in the Philippines -- we met an invasion on a small island the next day. But we operated around the Philippines and the suicide plane for a few days, and then we got caught in that typhoon, the one that sunk two or three destroyers, and almost another one or two.

They sent us out to convoy -- merchant ship convoy that was bringing supplies and equipment to the Philippines. And we rode out that typhoon. I had the watch in the engine room that night -- the top watch. And I dogged down all the hatches, all the engineering spaces, fire rooms and everything. We was down there there all night.

We didn't get out till 9 o'clock the next morning, 900 the next morning. We rolled -- I logged a roll of 68 degrees. Our destroyer -- my destroyer had (true) Ship and we was pretty heavy in the water. We rode it out pretty good, but it was a terrible storm. After that, we made a invasion of Lingayen Gulf in the Philippines. And we escorted -- that Lingayen Gulf, there was more suicide planes -- there were ships hit and everything. And we shelled the Japanese emplacement guns along the shore of the gulf all the way down one side and up the other, everything.

But when that was over, we went back to Lete Gulf -- the mouth of Lete Gulf -- and, I don't know, maybe the next two or three days, they was getting ready for the invasion of Okinawa. I believe the Iwo Jima campaign was in between. But I -- we didn't take part in that. They sent us to go down south of the equator to Guadalcanal, to training with the Marines. So this was the six-Marine division that was going to be -- landed in Okinawa later on. We trained with them in Okinawa until late March of 1945.

In late March, loaded everybody aboard the transport. My destroyer and two or three other destroyers escorted that group to Okinawa. We invaded Okinawa on the first day of April, 1945, April Fools Day. We started to get lot of action with suicide planes. On the -- everything went fairly good. The fighting was intense on the beach with the Marines and the Army, but on the sixth of April, we had a tremendous attack.

Those suicide planes coming on us all day. We not only fought them, we helped fight fire on ships that they hit and everything. But we managed to get through that without any hits on ourselves. We did a lot of firing. I don't know. We helped shoot down some planes. They sent us out on picket duty the next day to take the place of ships that had been hit by suicide planes on picket duty.

We made out till the ninth of April. The ninth of April, we got it. Four or five of them came down on us. We got them all. Two of us -- two suicide planes hit us. We shot the engine out of one and a bomb, and the fuselage flew into the bowel which didn't do too much damage. But then, another one followed it, and we got him on fire, but he hit us right at the water line in the starboard mess hall. Not the whole 16 feet long and eight feet tall.

We took in a lot of water, but the captain run the ship around in a circle and kept it heeled over. Luckily, the opening that had been into the ship was a little above the water line so we didn't take too much water, and everything. But we -- the engine went down through the the mess hall deck and made a big whole into an oil tank, so we was getting oil and fire. But we put out the fire.

Our emergency Diesel engine room was down there and it knocked the Diesel engine out, everything. We had -- I had one man down there on watch, but he was sitting right behind the Diesel engine, and the engine protected him. But he was oil all over. He didn't know what he was doing. He was sort of out wandering around on his feet. And I could see he was gonna fall down that hole into an oil tank.

I had my telephone talker call the main engine room and find out if all the electric power was off forward, and when I found out it was, I went down into that compartment, and another guy and my gang, another sailor and my gang followed me down there. We rounded up that boy that was oil-soaked out on his feet, and we brought him back, and finally got him up out of there.

That took in -- that just about did us in for the war there, because we was sent back to the -- We eventually -- they put us in the back channel, and we was attacked by Japs floating out with log rafts throwing hand grenades aboard. They managed to board one or two ships. But they put a smoke screen over us to protect us from the air. We patched up the hole and welded sheet metal over it.

Finally got under way and headed for the States. We hit Pearl Harbor and fixed the ship up a little bit better, and went to Seattle where we got repaired, fixed up, oh, probably a couple of months. They sent us to San Diego. While I was in San Diego, that's when we got word that the Japanese had agreed to surrender. I believe it was the 14th of August, 1945. We was in San Diego.

They sent us back -- we went back to Hawaii and headed back for the Japanese islands for occupation. But they sent my ship and several other destroyers and several battle ships and other -- clear Panama, and then up to New York where, in a course of time, they put us all out of commission. That was the end of the war for all of us.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: Your ship went into the New York group Atlantic Reserve Fleet?

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: Yeah. They scrapped -- I found out all them destroyers -- they scrapped them.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: That's right. That's the same place they pulled the Franklin -- they pulled the Franklin into New York.

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: You know, it was really torn up and they brought her over to Bayone, which was all the ships of that area, World War Two, were placed. And they call it the reserve (?and moth balls?).

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: I never will forget going into New York Harbor. I had the watch in the engine room, but I got relieved and I came up out of the engine room, and it was just after dark. And there was the Statue of Liberty, all lit up.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: Beautiful.

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: I never saw anything more that struck me as being more beautiful in my life: That Statute of Liberty. And the war was over.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: Well, you know Walt, that Statute of Liberty what you, and hundreds of thousands other military people went through in World War Two, is conducive to that Statute of Liberty. That means --

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: Oh, it struck me all the way. Statute of Liberty stands for "liberty."

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: And we had put four years of fighting a war for liberty.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: So, you know, it really impressed me very much. I stood there and watched it all the way into the harbor.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: Yup. It's a beautiful sight.

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: Yes, it was.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: Well Walt, we sure thank you for sharing your experiences with us. I particularly enjoyed -- because of your -- because of the destroyers that you were on.

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: I was on five destroyers in my career and I could equate to every time you mentioned something about the destroyers you were on. Of course, mine were all post-World War Two.

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: I didn't go in until 1947. When you started talking about destroyers, I don't know if you noticed my eyes light up or not. {Laughter}

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: Well, I was on several destroyers, but after the war, I was on auxiliary ships -- transports -- bringing troops back. I stayed in the Navy til 1960. Well, I got into the Korean War. The Korean War, I was an aviation supply ship, the Jupiter, for a while. Then I went to the heavy cruiser.

Then I went back to the -- flew back to the States and went to air conditioning school -- refrigeration/air-conditioning school, and then I flew right back out to Yakusca, Japan, and there I went aboard the Bummerton, heavy cruiser, CA 130. And I did the rest of the Korean War on that, and came back to the States and -- supposed to go to instructor machinist's school in the Naval Training Center, and I got down there and found myself down to the south grinder, pushing a rifle to become a company commander, a recruit friend. I did three years of that. Then I went back to the sea and my last ship was the Tortuga LSD 26, Landing Ship Dock.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: Landing Ship Dock.

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: Yeah. I got my retirement papers off the gang way. I didn't care about that shore-duty stuff anyway.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: That's not a man of war?

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: Well, again, thanks Walt. We appreciate it.

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: Yeah. [The following material is included on the tape.]

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: Oh, well, I guess I did. That ship -- that airplane machine gun bullet went right through my front fender and got my tire.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: Yeah, he did.

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: Well, all right.

sp.speaker: Walter Stevens
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Emmet Reed
sp.p: Thank you very much, Walt.
